subject: humanities
passage: In traditional Japanese indigo dyeing, or aizome, the blue does not come from a ready-made dye. Indigo leaves are first composted for months into a dark material called sukumo, which is then placed in a vat with lye made from wood ash. There, bacteria convert the insoluble indigo into a form that can soak into cloth; when the cloth is lifted out, contact with air turns it blue. Because the bacteria must be kept alive, dyers speak of feeding the vat and judge its condition by its smell and the look of its surface foam, and a neglected vat can fail entirely. Chemical agents can perform the same conversion in hours, yet many workshops still prefer the slower method.
stem: Which choice best states the main idea of the text?

choices.A: Traditional aizome relies on a living fermentation that dyers must tend with great care.
choices.B: Chemical agents have now largely replaced bacteria in Japan's traditional indigo workshops.
choices.C: Cloth dyed in an aizome vat turns blue only after it is lifted out and exposed to air.
choices.D: The slow aizome method produces deeper shades of blue than any chemical process can.

explanation.why: The text explains that aizome depends on bacteria in the vat, which "must be kept alive": dyers "feed" the vat, check its smell and foam, and risk losing it if it is neglected. The last sentence adds that many workshops still choose this slow, living process. The main idea is that aizome depends on carefully tended fermentation.
explanation.A: Correct. This sums up the text's focus: the bacteria-driven process and the care needed to keep it working.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says many workshops "still prefer the slower method," which contradicts this choice.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This is one step in the process, not the point of the whole text.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text never compares the depth of color produced by the two methods.
